title_en: Fragments on the Second Letter to the Thessalonians
author: Severian of Gabala
addressee: Christian readers, especially those troubled by persecution and speculation about Christ's return
occasion: Severian comments on 2 Thessalonians to console believers suffering persecution and to correct mistaken expectations about the timing and manner of Christ's second coming, especially fears stirred by false prophecy and forged letters.
argument: Paul writes to comfort the Thessalonians in persecution by reminding them of God's just recompense: punishment for the wicked and reward for the saints. He corrects their alarm about the day of the Lord by teaching that the rebellion and the man of lawlessness must come first. Severian explains that the devil has long been preparing idolatry and heresies as scaffolding for his own worship, and that the Holy Spirit currently restrains the lawless one until the appointed time. When Christ appears, he will destroy the lawless one by the breath of his mouth, and the devil's counterfeit incarnation will be undone.

outline.move: Introduces the letter as consolation amid persecution and correction of wrong expectations about the second coming, then comments on 2 Thess 1:3–2:4.
Explains the man of lawlessness as the antichrist who will exalt himself above every idol and heresy, and describes how the devil has long prepared these errors as scaffolding for his own worship.

Continues the scaffolding image, identifies the restrainer as the Holy Spirit, and shows that the mystery of lawlessness was already at work in apostolic times through schisms and heresies such as those of Mani and Marcion.

Cites Isaiah and Malachi on the destruction of the lawless one, explains that Christ's appearing abolishes the devil, and argues against the Apollinarians and Arians that the devil's counterfeit incarnation proves the Word assumed a complete human being.

key_terms.sense: The rebellion or falling away that must come before the day of the Lord.
The man of lawlessness, identified with the antichrist.
The antichrist, the deceiver who will come before Christ's return.
The coming or appearing of Christ, and by imitation the counterfeit coming of Satan.
The manifestation or appearing of Christ that destroys the lawless one.
The restraining power, identified as the Holy Spirit, that holds back the lawless one.
The hidden working of lawlessness already active in the apostolic age.
Idolatry, which the devil established and will later overthrow.
Heresies or sects that the devil uses as preparation for his own worship.
The scaffolding or support framework for an arch, used as an image for heresies preparing the devil's worship.
The Holy Spirit, who restrains the coming of the lawless one.
The working or power of Satan by which the lawless one comes.

scripture: Severian cites the Greek Old Testament, using LXX book names and Psalm numbering. Isaiah and Malachi are cited by name; Malachi is called 'the last of the prophets.' Modern citations should use standard English Bible names and numbering, noting LXX usage where it differs.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is uncertain.
The original extent and arrangement of the commentary is uncertain because the text survives only as catena fragments.
The precise identity of the 'last of the prophets' is inferred as Malachi from the quoted verses, but the source does not name him directly.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul: 'The apostle who wrote 2 Thessalonians and is quoted throughout.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul is not named in the fragments; he is inferred as the author of 2 Thessalonians but never explicitly identified by name in the source text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul (quoted Scripture): 'Quotations from 2 Thessalonians and the prophets are introduced by phrases such as 'he says' or by direct citation.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: Quotations from 2 Thessalonians are introduced with phrases like 'Παραινεῖ αὐτοὺς' (he exhorts them) and 'φησίν' (he says), but the speaker is never identified as 'Paul' by name in the source.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Isaiah (quoted prophet): 'Introduced as what Isaiah said beforehand.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: Isaiah is introduced as 'Ἡσαΐας προλαβὼν εἶπεν' (Isaiah said beforehand), but the source does not present this as a 'quoted prophet' voice distinct from Severian's commentary; it is Severian citing Isaiah.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The last of the prophets (identified by inference as Malachi): 'Referred to as 'the last of the prophets' (ὑστέρου τῶν προφητῶν) without being named directly.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says 'διὰ τοῦ ὑστέρου τῶν προφητῶν' (through the latter/last of the prophets), not 'ὑστέρου τῶν προφητῶν' as a standalone title. The brief's rendering as 'the last of the prophets' with definite article is slightly inaccurate; it is 'the latter/last of the prophets' in a partitive sense.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Severian explains that the devil has long been preparing idolatry and heresies as scaffolding for his own worship
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὥσπερ ὑποσκευὴ ἁψῖδος, οὕτως αἱ αἱρέσεις...ὑποσκευὴ λύεται, καὶ μένει μόνη ἡ ἁψὶς στερεά
_unresolved_facts.fix: The image is more precisely that heresies are 'scaffolding' (ὑποσκευή) for an arch (ἁψίς), with the devil's own worship being the completed arch, not merely 'his own worship' in a general sense. The scaffolding falls away when the arch is completed.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-close: 'argues against the Apollinarians and Arians that the devil's counterfeit incarnation proves the Word assumed a complete human being'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τοῦτο ὤφειλεν πεῖσαι τοὺς Ἀπολιναρίδας καὶ τοὺς Ἀριανούς, ὅτι ὅλον ἄνθρωπον ἀνέλαβεν ὁ θεὸς λόγος
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says 'this ought to have persuaded' (ὤφειλεν πεῖσαι), not that it actively argues against them. The rhetorical force is that the argument should convince them, not that Severian is directly addressing or polemicizing against them in this text.
